questions.prompt: What is a deontological moral theory, on his account?
choices: A One that ranks acts solely by total happiness produced.
B One focusing on what happens before/in the action’s character—duty/rules rather than outcomes alone.
C One that denies any moral evaluation of actions.
D One that only studies evolutionary history.
questions.explain: Deontology centers duty and act character.

questions.prompt: Kant’s Groundwork opens by claiming nothing is good without qualification except:
choices: A Pleasure and wealth.
B A good will.
C Civic popularity.
D Scientific genius alone.
questions.explain: Only a good will is good without qualification.

questions.prompt: For Kant, a good will primarily:
choices: A Equals being nice and generous as feelings.
B Acts from universal considerations / duty, not merely from inclination.
C Maximizes net utility.
D Follows local custom without reflection.
questions.explain: Good will acts on universal duty-based considerations.

questions.prompt: A categorical imperative, unlike a hypothetical one:
choices: A Applies only if you already want a particular goal.
B Commands independently of goals, desires, and circumstances—universally.
C Is only aesthetic advice.
D Never applies to promising.
questions.explain: Categorical imperatives apply universally, independent of contingent ends.

questions.prompt: In the false-promising example, Kant’s test centers on:
choices: A Whether you get caught empirically.
B Universalizing the maxim and seeing the contradiction as a universal law.
C How much utility the loan produces.
D Whether the lender is wealthy.
questions.explain: Universalize the maxim of false promising.
